articles.title: George Michael's Faith guitar sells for £180k after auction row
articles.text:
The guitar George Michael performed with in his 1987 Faith music video has sold for £180,000 at auction, after a row over the sale of memorabilia related to the singer.

The guitar was one of more than 30 items auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant. The sale fetched a total of £238,000 excluding buyers' premium.

Bailey died in 2014 and the items were sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Belcher declined to comment.

Sworders chairman Guy Schooling said Belcher had been "nothing but delightful" during their interactions over the past two-and-a-half years.

"There are two ways of looking at this - it can be cashing in, or it can be a bit of a memorial and a tribute to Siobhan, and that's the way we've looked at it," he told BBC News.

The auction house billed the 32 lots, including signed photographs, invitations to events and presentation CDs and discs, as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.

Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.

There is no suggestion that Belcher did not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.

Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.

In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considered the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name was "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".

He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" was "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".

Bailey asked that the auction should not go ahead, or be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.

Siobhan Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.

She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.

"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.

"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."

The guitar was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.

The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.

Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".

£180,000 - The Rockabilly Rebel guitar from the Faith video, with original hardshell case and leather guitar strap

£7,000 - A Queen Five Live EP sleeve signed by Brian May, John Deacon, Roger Taylor, George Michael and Lisa Stansfield

£5,000 - A Faith Tour ringbound itinerary from George Michael's 1988 world tour

£4,800 - A presentation CD of George Michael's Older

£4,500 - A gold disc of Wham!'s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go

£4,200 - A gold disc of George Michael's I Want Your Sex

Other items on sale included a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Andrew Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.

"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.

Speaking before Thursday's auction, he said "she would never have consented" to it, adding that the sale "breaks my heart".

"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax [tour itinerary] and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.

Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".

He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".

Bailey acknowledged that Belcher had a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

George Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.

articles.title: Jump scares, leather gloves and squeaking moth noises: theatre horror masters on how they make their shows so scary
articles.text:
It was 1am. Total darkness. Locking up a wedding venue, Sam Beech’s car sensor went off: there was something behind him. “It went on for half an hour,” the writer and director recalls, “on the front bumper, then round the back. But every time I looked, there was nothing.” It kept going, snuffling around the car. So he stopped looking. “I thought: ‘If I don’t look behind me, it won’t get me.’” Since then, Beech, the creator of one of a plethora of horror shows currently haunting the stage, admits, “I don’t like driving in the dark”.

Beech’s experience was eerily similar to a scene in Andy Nyman’s hit 2010 play Ghost Stories, which Beech had seen four times, so the gnarly end the character had met on stage filled his mind when the sensor went off in the dark. Now, the uncanny experience has fed into his own new horror show Blackout (touring the UK to 27 February), which uses everything that made him so scared that night: the quiet, the absence, the idea of something lurking in the shadows. “It’s the Jaws effect,” says Chris Fisher, the illusions designer behind the stage show of Paranormal Activity (at London Ambassador’s theatre to 27 February, and touring the UK), which had me sheepishly checking under my bed for several nights and stopped just short of nightmares. “It’s scarier to see the fin and hear the music,” Fisher says, “than it is to see the mechanical head of the shark.”

On stages across the country, theatre-makers are hoping to make their audiences grab the arms of strangers next to them. But it’s easy to go wrong with horror, Fisher says: “It often goes too far, too hammy. Too – and I say this affectionately – Blithe Spirit.” But when you get it right, he says, discounting Noël Coward’s farce about an eccentric clairvoyant, “people leave with a newfound understanding of what theatre can do”.

For years, 1987’s The Woman in Black was the reigning champion of achieving a proper nail-biting scare on stage. On a sparse set, the show invited the audience to imagine a pony and trap as the story set off, priming them, like Beech’s stalking shadow and Fisher’s Jaws theory, to fill in the gaps for themselves. It was unrivalled for years, but recently, perhaps kicked off by the success of Ghost Stories, there’s been an increasing flood of shows trying to eke out new ideas of horror plays. The campily satisfying haunted house thriller 2:22: A Ghost Story is ever-touring and the hallucinatory Stranger Things: The First Shadow (which also features Fisher’s illusions) is going strong in London’s West End. Farther west in the city, at the Bush theatre, Mei Leng Yew’s recent debut The Hungry Ghost played with Chinese traditions and queer obsession to create a nightmarish story of possession. Going down the route of psychological horror, the immersive touring experience Sins uses audience participation to determine what happens on stage. This Halloween season, the ghosts and ghouls have busy schedules.

“Maybe 2.22 was so successful that it just initiated a cascade,” says comedian Kirsty Mann, who tests her audience’s belief in ghosts with a true tale of her haunted house in the comedy-horror Corpse, which is coming to London’s Soho theatre in February after an Edinburgh fringe run. “These things come in cycles,” she says. “But people go to the theatre for escapism and horror is the ultimate escapism. There’s so much awfulness in the world right now, people are turning more to the fantastic, and with horror, you’re not just following the story. You’re totally separated from reality.” Now, finding the scariest night out possible has become “almost a drug”, Fisher says, for audiences chasing the high of the collective fright. “It’s like being on a rollercoaster,” says Mann, who saw Paranormal Activity three times in one month.

The line between successful scare and unimpressed shrug is a fine one. “It’s a bit like comedy,” says Carolyn Downing, sound designer on The Silence of the Lambs, the stage adaptation of the psycho-killer movie that is touring the UK to 26 June. “It has to be super-precise. It only takes a mistimed or misaligned moment, and your brain’s quick enough to go: ‘I didn’t believe that.’” The success of that minuscule moment relies on the atmosphere created by dozens of people backstage. “It’s all about the buildup,” Downing says. Achieving the perfect jump scare requires the increase in tension, the wrongfooting, and the offbeat fright just as you’ve relaxed. “It won’t scare you if you’re half expecting it,” she says.

Horror works best, set designer Ti Green believes, “when your understanding of the rules are pulled apart”. For the stage adaptation of Shirley Jackon’s 1959 gothic novel The Haunting of Hill House, Green wanted to build a world that looked solid and dependable. “That’s the first step,” she says. “The second is to dismantle everyone’s sense of safety.” Jackson’s story is a quintessential haunted house, with a group of ghost seekers wandering around a decrepit mansion. Paying homage to Jackson’s description of “Hill House, not sane”, much of Green’s set is made of translucent gauze, so depth and vision can play with the idea that everything is constantly in flux, making it feel, she says, “as if the house is doing it, not as if the theatre is doing it”.

In Blackout, Beech aims for the opposite effect: he wants the theatre itself to feel haunted. Having created the award-winning Statfold Scream Park, he is moving his experience in horror events on stage with this touring show that plays in each venue for just one night. “Five hundred people walk into a theatre and choose to accept something they know isn’t real,” he says, setting up the show, which is framed as a rehearsal. With the audience as ghosts to the action, Blackout aims to dissect and strengthen the classic tropes of horror: “darkness, silence, negative space”. As in The Woman in Black, the agreement to suspend disbelief allows the paranormal to take a step closer.

These conventions of horror on stage are not cheat codes. “Anyone can go and buy a magic trick and try to perform it,” Fisher says, “but they’re not actually doing real magic. It’s all about how you present it, what story you put with it. It’s the same with horror.” Many of the principles of good illusion – and good horror – have remained largely unchanged over time. “For Paranormal Activity, I went back to the ways that Victorian magicians or spiritualists would have done it,” Fisher says. “The majority of the illusions could have been used for hundreds of years.”

Illusions such as Fisher’s have become a significant selling point for modern horror on stage, perhaps, as Mann suggests, because they give a “wow factor” that is hard to recreate on screen with the ubiquitous powers of AI and CGI. “In live theatre, if you pull off an amazing trick,” she says, “you can have that moment of, ‘Holy shit, how did they do that?’”

Maximising the bodily experience of sharing the space, theatre has the opportunity to be even scarier than film, allowing the fear to slip off the stage and follow you home. “The really scary stuff is when it taps into a deep fear you have,” says Mann. In Corpse, which uses minimal set and choice illusions by John Bulleid, she pushes on the bruise of the feeling: this could happen to me.

Other shows have the challenge of a direct comparison with their originals; that Paranormal Activity, The Silence of the Lambs and The Haunting of Hill House, which is touring the UK to 21 November, are all adaptations says something of the endurance of spooky stories. For The Silence of the Lambs, Downing felt a responsibility to achieve the iconic sound of moths, which marks a significant turning point in the story. Using foley techniques, she’s previously made the sound of birds with flapping leather gloves, but the moths needed to be smaller and finer. Her list of moth-making ingredients includes rustling leaves, swooshing paper, rubbed hands and the real recorded squeaking of death’s-head hawkmoths. “The juiciness of horror is that you can zoom in on sound,” she says, “make it feel visceral and intense.”

This is key; a horror play has to be felt. So much of that feeling being handed over to the audience, Fisher says, is down to the actors. “Like with illusion, when you see something again and again, you become a bit jaded with it. It’s the same thing with horror scares. It’s so important to keep those reactions as if they are experiencing it for the first time, because that’s what we’re doing.”

Halloween in the UK is growing. “We’re about 10 or 15 years behind America,” says Beech. “I think that’s probably the same with horror shows and audience appetite.” As demand grows, so do these theatre-makers’ ambitions. “I want to keep pushing it,” says Fisher. When the Paranormal Activity team recently locked the show in New York, he says, “we all sat down for dinner, together for the first time in months, and were like, ‘What shall we do next?’” He nods to me: “Make sure you have those nightmares.”

articles.title: ‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bed
articles.text:
Aidan Turner has a tactical beard. For the last two decades or so, the actor has found himself in roles that have made him a smouldering pin-up. Audiences really love to look at him. You can buy mugs that say, “Today I don’t feel like doing anything … except Aidan Turner.” There are entire Reddit forums dedicated to sharing photographs of him looking hot. He knows this about himself, just like he knows that people want to ask him about it. “I do get asked these questions,” he says, a little wearily. “I do get the, you know, word ‘smoulder’ or ‘sexy’, and all that kind of shit.” So right now, he has a full beard, in the hope that he will not be accused of, for example, smouldering. “I thought it wouldn’t happen so much with the beard,” he sighs. “I thought I could get away with it. I was going for ‘dad’.”

The job of actors is to sell a story as well as they possibly can, and over the years plenty of the stories that Turner has sold have involved romance and sex. He appeared in Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National Theatre in London this summer, and even the New Yorker noted how much he smoulders. In some ways, Turner is one of those male performers who is, well, a little bit objectified. The fact that he is a good actor, and also known for being sexy, places him in a peculiar bind. If he doesn’t gamely play along, if he points out that he’s getting a bit tired of it actually, then he risks being seen as a killjoy. Sure, there are worse burdens to bear, but at times the star of Poldark and Rivals finds himself in a curious position.

Turner is 43 now. (He is literally a dad – he and his wife, the American actor Caitlin FitzGerald, have got a small son.) His early roles showed off his ability to handsomely, pensively brood. He was a vampire in the sci-fi series Being Human, and played Dante Gabriel Rossetti in Desperate Romantics, writing moody poetry in soft light. Then, in 2015, he starred in the BBC’s hugely popular adaptation of Poldark, which turned him into a household name. As Ross Poldark, an 18th-century soldier, he loved, fought and, very famously, swung a scythe. The attention that came with it made his career, but it also put him off sexy roles for a while. Then a few years later, Rivals came along.

Rivals is outrageously fun and smutty. It adapts Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire Chronicles novels, the kind of books that would once have been known as bonkbusters, into big, brash television. In her fictionalised version of the Cotswolds in the 1980s, Cooper brought together aristocrats, MPs and cut‑throat television executives. Everyone is having sex with everyone; everyone is ready to stab their neighbour in their back, and probably have sex with them at the same time. Everyone, that is, except Turner’s character, Declan O’Hara, a serious‑minded broadcast journalist who is unusually faithful to his wife, Maud – and also dashingly handsome. So here Turner is again, fielding questions about intimacy coordinators, sex scenes and his very full moustache.

The moustache was his idea. “I say it was my idea,” he begins, then corrects himself. “It fucking was my idea.” Turner swears like it is going out of fashion. He has just finished today’s photoshoot, so we have gone to find a quiet spot to chat, and have ended up in a basement, surrounded by bikes and cleaning products and tools. He is out of the fancy clothes and back in his east London dad uniform of white T-shirt, navy chore jacket and jeans. He explains that he had turned up for the Rivals job with a full beard, and if they were going to shave it off, he told them, he had no intention of using a stick-on prosthetic. “You end up eating hairs all day and if you smile it falls off,” he says. “I think everyone on set has now learned the lesson of no stickies.” So they shaved him down to a moustache first, and decided they liked it, and that’s what stuck. It also gave Declan a bit more gravitas. “I don’t want to make this about getting into character or anything. All that stuff gives me the creeps, actors talking about that,” he says, squirming. “But [the moustache] is really helpful, because Declan feels older to me. Like, he’s a bit more of a grownup than I am.” Turner grew up in Dublin and has the accent to prove it, but Declan has a Westmeath accent, a bit deeper than his own, which he borrowed from his father, Pearse. “So with that, and the geography teacher outfits, everything feels more mature.”

Rivals has been a juggernaut for all involved. The TV series is nostalgic and knowing, horny and hilarious, but the new episodes find the show in a more gloomy mood. It opens with a funeral – don’t panic; I counted, and it only takes 15 minutes to get to a sex scene – and trouble is brewing for Declan and Maud’s marriage. “It’s a big one,” Turner nods, though spoiler etiquette dictates he cannot say too much.

The fact that Rivals can swing so comfortably between profound grief, camp backstabbing and joyful infidelity gives it a very particular tone. Why does Turner think that audiences have lapped it up? “I mean, I was born in ’83, and there is this yearning for that nostalgia, I suppose. And Jilly Cooper has a certain tone. She was looked over for many years. It was seen as this low-rent, smutty kind of literature, and I don’t know if a lot of people gave it a chance. That doesn’t seem to be the case any more.” He has noticed that it appeals to lots of age groups, and for the first time in a while people in their 20s are coming up to him in the street. “Rivals is funny, and it knows exactly what it is,” he offers. “It’s unapologetic. It’s on the front foot and it’s out there, going, this is what we’re doing, this is who we are.”

Cooper was heavily involved in the first season, and they were in the middle of shooting the second when the author died suddenly, at the age of 88. Turner has fond memories of her. “She was famous for throwing these parties at her house in the Cotswolds that were just exactly what you would imagine,” Turner says. “They were so much fun. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhere. She was so spirited.” He was filming the immediate aftermath of those funeral scenes when he sensed that something was going on. “It was eerie already, and I mentioned to Victoria [Smurfit, who plays Maud] that this feels weird. It feels very dark, and, like, not Rivals. And then we took a break, and I knew something was up.” The line producer broke the news to the cast that Cooper had died.

Five weeks earlier, Turner says, he had been at one of those famous parties. “And she was making speeches and drinking champagne and introducing me to people. She was her brilliant, funny, filthy self.” Cooper would often swing by the set. “I’m just glad that she got a chance to see the show, to see where it was going and how it was looking, and she was really proud of it.”

Given the amount of sex involved in Rivals, it is no surprise that they use intimacy coordinators to assist with the choreography. Turner remembers the time before intimacy coordinators were commonplace, and he finds it much better, and much easier, now that they are readily available on sets. In the past, he remembers working with directors who were hands-off or awkward when it came to sex scenes. “They just kind of leave it to you. And I don’t know whether that’s a really good thing, you know, because it’s, like, what the fuck do we do? And is this OK? And does this work?” Having a professional who is there to figure that out is really useful. “I think it’s important, especially in a show like this, to sell the scene and to do what we’re doing, because there are so many different types of sex in this show. It helps us a lot.”

Turner was in his early 30s when he got the lead in Poldark, the BBC’s second adaptation of the Winston Graham novels, about a soldier returning home from the American revolutionary war. It turned you into a pin-up, I suggest. He takes a breath so deep that it could fill a Cornish tin mine. “I suppose they were positioning Ross to be that,” he concedes, carefully. “There was a sex in Ross, wasn’t there, I suppose,” he says, with a chuckle, “that previously wasn’t there.” He mentions the photograph of him taken behind the scenes, in a field, topless, with a scythe. For the last 10 years, it has appeared again and again, which, he says, is “all quite embarrassing. It kind of went everywhere.” In it, Turner is being touched up by the show’s makeup artist Jacqui Fowler, who is often airbrushed out of the shot, much to his disdain. “She’s there with the makeup brush, brilliant Jacqui, and I don’t know what she’s doing … ”

Was she painting his muscles? (I meant enhancing them, rather than adding them.) “No! That was something I fucking worked hard for,” he laughs. “I was 12 years younger. It was probably a lot easier to get in shape. But I was, like, no, this guy is a farmer. He’s on the horse all the time. We never really see him eating. When he is, it’s fucking gruel. He’s probably quite lean.” So Turner decided that he needed to get in shape, too. As with the Rivals moustache, it was his idea to go topless in the scything scene, and he had no idea that it would still be talked about a decade later. “I made some friends on the show that I’m still friends with now, and I’m proud of it. It had a really strong audience, and we tried to do something different with it, and I think we did. But all of that stuff was embarrassing, because it just kind of follows you around a little bit. But it might not have been successful if we didn’t have any of that at all.”

For a few years afterwards – until Rivals, in fact – Turner resisted taking roles that he knew would require him to be sexy. Did Poldark put him off? “It did, yeah,” he says. In photoshoots now, for example, he might politely decline to pose in a way that seems suggestive. “It just feels different, at 43, and being a dad,” he shrugs. Then again, he admits, he is here to talk about Rivals. Also, he has just finished Les Liaisons Dangereuses, that famously sex-focused play, in which his character Valmont manipulates women into bed, for sport and for the sheer sociopathic thrill of it. “And you’re, like, well, I mean, you’re asking for it, dude!” he laughs. He is nothing if not self-aware. “But then, I feel like this sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end. Right? Tell me it’s done.” I think that’s up to him. “For sure, and it is. But the roles are getting more interesting, and less about … that.”

Turner has never done social media and says he has never felt any pressure to sign up to it. “No. You would definitely get more free shit if you had a few million followers on Instagram. I do meet people and I’m, like, where did you get that? And they’re, like, oh, it got sent to me.” But he knows it’s not worth it. “I don’t need those trainers. Most people I know are on it, but I don’t really want to share those things. And I don’t think I’d be very good at doing it. I would probably get it wrong. I’d probably either overshare, or not do it enough.”

Turner does not strike me as an oversharer. He mentions early mornings taking his son to school after a late night at the theatre, or trips with him to the West End to see The Lion King and Paddington, but otherwise he is tight-lipped on life outside work. “I draw the line at the personal stuff. And plus, I’ve always just felt, like, who wants to hear from me? I always felt that, in the early days of Twitter or X or whatever. It takes so much confidence, doesn’t it, to go, ‘People want to hear exactly what I have to say in this sentence.’ Wow. The balls on that. Jesus. I’d love some of that courage.”

When not being forced to examine the embarrassment of being objectified as a man in your 40s by horrible, intrusive journalists, Turner is great company. He is funny; he is as charming, as you might expect; and he is more than happy to discuss big, state‑of-the-world stuff. Take this morning. He was listening to a podcast about Meta’s new AI assistant, he says. “They will do shit for you. They’ll order food and deliver it to a friend of yours, and they’ll make sure that if you want to get paid, you’ll get paid, and they’ll make sure your mortgage gets done every month, and they’ll do everything. But you’ve just got to give them all of you.” He realised, for the first time, that he was scared of what might happen next. “There could be a moment where it’s, like, no, sorry, Aidan, there is no money for you. We need that money for a datacentre.” The podcast talked about how helpful AI could be, as well as how destructive. “But this has already been downloaded by millions of people, and I’m, like, we’re walking straight into this fire, aren’t we? This might be coming for us faster than I thought.”

Does he worry about AI coming for his job? The late Gene Wilder’s voice has been reactivated for a Netflix reality show; Tilly Norwood, the world’s first AI actor, has been unleashed on Hollywood, to middling results. “It will get better and better, and it’s about how comfortable we are when it does get amazing and we can’t tell the difference,” he says. “I don’t know whether I want to read a novel from an AI author. I want the human. I want the connection.” Maybe he is showing his age, he says, “but I don’t want to write us off yet. I don’t want a painting that’s been generated by AI. I want to see oil and canvas and acrylic. Call me old school, but I want the humans to win that battle.”

Turner lives in London now, with FitzGerald and their son. He moved to the city in his 20s, after a few years of doing theatre in Dublin. “My first TV job brought me over, and I never really went back,” he says. “I love London. For me, it’s still one of the most exciting cities in the world.” The couple have lived in the US for short periods of time, too, though neither was keen on settling there. For political reasons? “I’m not going to lie. Guns scare me, and we have a young child, and I don’t want to worry about that every day. I know we have our own problems in this country, but the guns thing scares me. I think the healthcare system is completely fucked [in America]. God forbid you’re not very wealthy, because if you get sick and you don’t have much money, or even if you’re doing all right, it will take everything. That just seems crazy to me.”

Turner grew up in Clondalkin, in the west of County Dublin, with his brother and his parents. “We were a working-class family. My dad retired a few years ago, but he was an electrician, and my mum is an accountant.” He had a grandmother who did amateur dramatics, but otherwise there was no history of performing in the family. When Turner realised he wanted to go to drama school, at 18, “there was a certain mould being broken, there”. But, he says, he did have some experience of being on stage. “It would be remiss of me not to say that there was an unusual part of my childhood where I danced,” he begins.

He was not just a casual dancer. He danced ballroom and Latin American from the age of six to 17, and at one point he came third in the All-Ireland dance championships. “That’s weird as fuck,” he laughs. “I mean, not odd, but just not the norm for a kid from west Dublin, which is quite poor. My mum and dad spent a lot of money to fund that.” He describes the world of competitive dancing in vivid detail. “There were trophies everywhere, and we went to a competition and it was tails and suits and numbers on the back, and fake tan and Elnett hairspray and pushy mums.

“I went to schools that were quite rough, and I danced right up until I was 17,” he continues. “And I told everyone!” Was he given a hard time for it? “I don’t think they believed me, that’s my theory.” He has seen old friends who have since read about his dancing years, and they told him that they didn’t think he was being serious. “These are working-class boys, who are 14, 15, and we’re all drinking cider on a Friday night and smoking cigarettes and doing whatever else. And you tell them that you’re away to Blackpool this weekend, that you dance, and they might believe you. But they don’t want to take part in this conversation. They move away. They still want to be your mate, but they don’t have the faculties to deal with this conversation.” He gave up dancing when his dance partner got injured, and while on a break, he applied on a whim for drama school. “I was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in there,” he says. Acting made him less self-conscious, and he knew straight away that it was the life for him.

Turner has roles coming up that take him beyond the heart-throb. He is waiting for work to start on Grendel, the live-action adaptation of the 1971 novel, which tells the story of Beowulf from the monster’s perspective. Is he playing a monster? “No, no, he’s a warrior. He’s a shit warrior,” he jokes. “I don’t even know how much I can talk about that. I hope it’s still happening.” He also plays the Apostle Andrew in Terrence Malick’s forthcoming biblical epic, about the life of Jesus Christ, currently known as The Way of the Wind, though Malick is, famously, not a fast worker, and it was filmed in 2019. “Surely it’s coming out soon? I don’t know,” he says.

But he has also, briefly, returned to The Diplomat, Netflix’s popular political thriller, reprising his role as the British spy Callum Ellis. And there is no denying it: Callum is a sexy guy. “Oh, come off it. I am not sexy in The Diplomat,” he says, firmly. “That is all you.” He really does think, or hope, that this era is almost behind him. “It must be coming to an end,” he says. But what if he’s got another 20 years of it left? “Oh no,” he says, laughing. Then groans, as if he cannot think of anything worse.

articles.title: The Celebrity Traitors final review – more muted but still thrilling to the last
articles.text:
They took it right down to the wire but in the end we finally got a moment of true treachery in this series of Celebrity Traitors where none of the contestants seemed to have understood the brief. Or the title. At the final round table, King Kenny turned on the queen and voted Maya – with her Cruella de Vil cheekbones but without the villainous heart to match – out.

As if that were not unexpected excitement enough at the end of a five-week, 10-show run whose record-breaking viewing figures have somewhat belied its comparatively muted nature, we had a last-minute wobble from Romesh that threw the endgame into turmoil. Turmoil! TURMOIL!

As Maya left, you see, a shimmering, furious vision in jade, she added to her goodbye, “Good luck. You’re going to need it.”

Romesh considered James Blunt to be uncharacteristically dismissive of what that might mean and – à la Nick Mohammed with Joe Marler last year – was suddenly convulsed by doubt and voted to banish the man who could not have been more clearly a Faithful than if he’d been … well, Joe Marler.

Blunt, who had remained so consummately untouched by self-doubt throughout the show despite being 100% wrong 32bn times – “God give me the confidence of a perfectly pleasant white man” could become his new family crest – was shattered by the volte-face.

Kenny, meanwhile, silently rejoiced because it left him in pole position to win. Until Bash – Bash, that tiny sweet wisp of a child! – stepped up, split the vote, talked sense into Romesh and got the last remaining Traitor banished instead.

Then it was just the three Faithfuls left, and all were set to call it quits and split the prize money three ways. Except there was one last chance for Blunt to be wrong again and so he looked once, looked twice, and seized it. And was duly voted off.

Perhaps “Consistency in all things” will do, in Latin, under a berk rampant. Bash and Romesh split their prize money between two charities for refugees and displaced persons. It was a result everyone could enjoy.

And it was some form of oblique justice for Leigh-Anne, who had only ever been cheering up Miranda with her impromptu choreography and it hurt all our hearts to see her suffering for it.

And if that last sentence makes no sense to you – well, that is sort of the point of The Traitors, in its celebrity incarnation or otherwise. You need to get into it. You have to commit to the run.

There’s no point dipping in and out – you either get to know the personalities, the ebbs and flows in popularity, the alliances made and broken, the tiny moments that become pivotal (or the huge blunders – hope you’re OK, Richard E G, or the massive curveballs – hi, James A, we’re still processing that one) and join in the fun, sign up to the temporary national pastime, or you don’t.

The latter type will piss and moan about its existence and the former will enjoy that rarest thing – a few hours of respite from the world that is too much with us, by immersion in a game that doesn’t matter and that harms precisely no one.

It’s true this season is unlikely to go down as a classic – too few twists, not enough suspense, too few metaphorical jugulars severed, not enough Celia Imrie farting in a shack – but it still got its main job done.

And left us with the hope that one day Maya will turn to politics, ideally on a joint ticket with Joe Lycett, rise again and come to rule us all.

articles.title: Yaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilarious
articles.text:
Halloween was once a simpler time, when neighbourhood kids would dress up as mythical serial killers, the undead or bedsheet-wearing ghosts. At some point, following America’s lead, it became sexy and cat-forward. It has now become a sort of conceptual art show. I’ve heard people this year planning to go to parties dressed as Erling Haaland, Prom Carrie (Prime Video edition) and Bad Bunny’s half-time Super Bowl show. It’s horrifying.

The perception of witches has evolved, too. Once understood to be a malignant version of the crone archetype, sympathy for witches has grown. They have been embraced as a feminist image of the older woman, free of patriarchal command and possessed of a powerful rage. In recent years, Maleficent, Elphaba from Wicked and Marvel’s Scarlet Witch have given witches a pop edge. Some of my most intense friends proudly wear slogan T-shirts proclaiming themselves descended from the witches whom society failed to burn.

Now, in swoops Yaga (Sat, 9pm, Sky Atlantic), a quasi-horror mystery series from Canadian streamer Crave. They are known for making Heated Rivalry (matching oversized jerseys? Huge Halloween outfit this year). Yaga is another genre-bender. It opens with a cocky detective, Charlie Rapp, arriving in the quiet fishing town of Whittock, present day. He’s investigating the disappearance of Henry Park, son of a wealthy local family. As the case grows violent, it brings evidence of cult activity to light, and increasingly hints at the existence of a dark, supernatural figure behind events.

To those unfamiliar with Slavic folklore, Baba Yaga is a forest-dwelling hag who lives in a hut on chicken’s feet, flies around in a pestle and mortar, and eats children. It is her voice that bookends every episode in a taunting monologue, though her exact involvement with Henry’s disappearance is a grisly little puzzle. I’m a few episodes in, and it’s still unclear if she is a literal character in the play or the embodiment of its theme: women being sick of men’s shit.

The men are certainly a rum bunch. Charlie Rapp is our hero – yet his credentials are questionable, and he flirts with every woman in town, including his police partner Carson. Henry Park – played by Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams – is vain, adulterous and given to druggy parties. Williams also plays Henry’s slippery roommate Logan. The show has fun with the unlikely physical resemblance between them, as when Logan answers the door to the surprised detectives. “I have brown eyes and glasses,” he explains with a straight face. He’s also naked under his overalls, FYI.

The women are formidable, including Clark Backo’s drily unimpressed take on police detective Carson. She’s introduced as a fan of romantasy (or what her superior officer describes as “fairy smut”). Carson is unenthusiastic about pursuing the case of the missing rich kid. “Billionaires aren’t real people,” she shrugs. Even more no-nonsense is Carrie-Anne Moss as an older, morally ambiguous osteo-academic. When Charlie sits beside her at a bar and asks what excites her, she replies: “Sex. And bones.”

Given the bones, and the overalls, you may be thinking: “Stuff the spooky business, are there hella sexy shenanigans?” Yes and no … The theme of Henry’s parties, which take place Gatsby-like in his absence, is Dark Solstice. Expect masked ball eroticism, fetish wear and debauchery and, elsewhere, an erotic encounter that had me laughing at the audacity. But it’s never wholesome fun. There are chicken bones in unexpected places, and Rapp in particular is haunted by horror imagery. While sex is on the menu, the male gaze is under the microscope.

Playwright-creator Kat Sandler has, so far, found room on the broom to make Yaga pointed but playful, and fun while tackling the darkest of subject matter. There are Ukrainian covers of pop songs, a hero who looks like a leather-trouser version of Tim Key, and Saltburn-esque parties. But what I really want, whisper it, is for an actual witch to appear, rather than the political idea of one. I’m basic, and like pointy hats. Will this be another Blair Witch situation? How far will the witch-tease go? I’m crossing my fingers and burying the hair of a bat.
